questions.text: In count_vowels you stored the vowels in a set. Why did you choose a set instead of a list or a plain string?

key_ideas: Checking membership in a set is fast, about constant time
Order and duplicates do not matter for a group of vowels
A list or string would also work for five letters, so the set mainly states the intent
expected.model_answer: I used a set because I only need to ask whether a letter is a vowel. Membership checks on a set are fast and the order of the vowels does not matter. A list or string would also work for just five letters, but a set shows the intent.

questions.text: In remove_duplicates, walk me through what seen and result hold after the loop has processed the list 3, 1, 3, 2.

key_ideas: result ends up as the list 3, 1, 2
The second 3 is skipped because it is already in seen
expected.model_answer: seen ends up as the set containing 3, 1 and 2, and result is the list 3, 1, 2. When the second 3 arrives the check says it is already in seen, so it is not added to result again.

questions.text: Two of your tests failed when the list contained other lists, like [[1], [1]]. Why did that fail, and how could you change your code to handle it?

key_ideas: Lists are unhashable, so they cannot be added to a set
The error is raised by the membership check or the add on seen
A fix is to track seen items in a list, or convert inner lists to tuples
expected.model_answer: A set needs hashable items and a list is not hashable, so checking or adding it to seen raises a TypeError. I could keep seen as a list, which is slower but works for any item, or convert inner lists to tuples before storing them.
